title: BCCI Fines Ranji-Capped TNPL Player Rs 1 Lakh for Using Mobile Phone During Match
excerpt: The Board of Control for Cricket in India penalized a Tamil Nadu player for breaching anti-corruption protocols by texting on his phone during a TNPL game, adding to the league's growing integrity concerns.
body:
• The BCCI's Anti-Corruption Unit fined a Ranji Trophy-capped Tamil Nadu Premier League player Rs 1 lakh for using a mobile phone during a match — reportedly to text his girlfriend
  • The breach violates strict anti-corruption protocols that prohibit players from carrying personal electronic devices in designated match areas
  • The incident comes amid a broader BCCI investigation into alleged corruption in the TNPL, with multiple players and coaches under the Anti-Corruption Unit's scanner
  • Cricket experts and former players say the proliferation of state T20 leagues has made integrity monitoring increasingly difficult

Phone Violation Draws Fine

The Board of Control for Cricket in India has fined a Ranji Trophy-capped player Rs 1 lakh after he was caught using a mobile phone during a Tamil Nadu Premier League match, multiple Indian media outlets reported. The player was reportedly texting his girlfriend when anti-corruption officials flagged the breach.

Under BCCI anti-corruption protocols, players are strictly prohibited from carrying personal electronic devices — particularly mobile phones — into designated match areas including dressing rooms and dugouts. The rule exists to prevent potential communication with bookmakers or other outside parties during live matches.

The player's identity has not been officially disclosed by the BCCI, though Indian media reports identified him as a first-class cricketer with Ranji Trophy experience. The Rs 1 lakh penalty and a formal warning were imposed after the Anti-Corruption Unit found the player's explanation unsatisfactory, according to reports in Hindustan Times and The Indian Express.

TNPL Under Broader Scrutiny

The fine adds to mounting integrity concerns surrounding the TNPL, India's prominent state-level T20 franchise cricket league. The BCCI's Anti-Corruption Unit has been probing links between players and bookies over alleged corruption in the league, with multiple first-class cricketers and at least two coaches coming under the scanner for suspected match-fixing.

Ajit Singh, head of the BCCI's ACU, told ESPNCricinfo that the inquiry involves tracking people who sent WhatsApp messages to players seeking match-related information. "It is an inquiry into who has made an approach. The players have told us we have received these messages, so it is not an inquiry against the player," Singh said.

The Tamil Nadu Cricket Association, which owns the league, appointed a committee to investigate the allegations but said it would refrain from making statements until the probe concludes. The TNCA said the league operates under the BCCI's Anti-Corruption Code and maintains a "zero-tolerance policy" toward any cricketer involved in malpractice.

State Leagues Face Integrity Challenge

The incident underscores the challenges of maintaining integrity standards across India's expanding ecosystem of state-level T20 leagues. Cricket legend Sunil Gavaskar has warned that the proliferation of these tournaments creates more opportunities for corruption, even as they serve as crucial talent pipelines for Indian cricket.

"Greed is something that is human. The best of societies still have criminals. In cricket also you will always have the odd person who will be swayed by greed," Gavaskar said, while stressing that technology makes it harder for cheats to hide.

The TNPL, launched in 2016, features eight franchises and has previously faced scrutiny. It has also produced several international cricketers, making it one of the more significant state leagues in Indian cricket.

What's Next

The BCCI's ongoing investigation into the TNPL is expected to produce a comprehensive report. If evidence of systematic corruption is found, the consequences could range from individual sanctions to structural changes in how state-level leagues are governed and monitored. The episode serves as a reminder that the battle for cricket's integrity extends well beyond the IPL.
